title: The only evidence that needle3 confidence supports act/confirm/refuse routing is a misread of its own data: the 0.55 belongs to a COMPLETE claim, not the 'no amount' one
claim_or_artifact: FINDINGS.md:138-140: "5 claims benchmarked: confidences `[0.98, 0.55, 0.77, 0.94, 0.99]`. The 0.55 was the one claim with **no amount** (\"third-party liability after a fall, no amount\") — the score dropped exactly where a human would pause." Repeated as a headline at FINDINGS.md:25 ("tool-calling + confidence gating fit 'act / confirm / refuse' routing") and FINDINGS.md:296 ("The strongest fit.").
problem: The confidences list is appended in query order. The no-amount query is the THIRD item, so it scored 0.768; the 0.549 belongs to the second item, "Policy AXA-2: fire damage in the garage on 5 Sept, 12000 euros." - a fully specified claim. So the one positive calibration observation in the paper is false, and what the data actually shows is a complete claim scoring lowest. Worse, experiment D never stored the model outputs or any gold label (only confidences and call counts), so correctness of the 5 calls is unknown, and it ran on the single shared `agent` that already had A1-A4 in its history - the same 'context bleed' the paper itself declares disqualifying in section 7 but never applies retroactively to section 4.3. On that shared agent an in-domain message (A4: "A customer wants to make a claim about their car.") was refused as "a general knowledge question" at confidence 1.0, which the paper does not report. Every data point where confidence AND correctness are both known argues against routing on the score: E2 wrong at 0.9929, E4 fabricated policy_number="800 euros" at 0.8729. There is no labelled triage set, no routing accuracy, no threshold sweep, no risk-coverage curve, no cost/latency model - yet triage is called the strongest fit.

title: Anonymisation answered 'Yes' from one English-language email with a one-slot-per-type schema; the test itself leaks a date of birth, no redaction was ever executed, and there is no recall/precision, no baseline, no French text, no round trip
claim_or_artifact: FINDINGS.md:28 "Can it anonymise data? | Yes — it extracts PII into typed fields on-device, which can drive a redaction step"; FINDINGS.md:131 "### 4.2 PII extraction (anonymisation feed) — excellent"; FINDINGS.md:275 "This is the same job Microsoft Presidio does"; artifact experiments/needle3_claims.py:95-108.
problem: (a) n=1. (b) The PII schema is six scalar strings (full_name, phone, email, address, policy_number, id_number), so any text with two people, two phones or a third party's name cannot be fully captured by construction - recall is structurally capped, which is the opposite of what a redaction gate needs. (c) The single test input contains "born 12/03/1980"; the schema has no DOB field and the recorded output has none, so the only anonymisation test in the paper would have leaked a quasi-identifier. (e) The input is English prose with French entities; no French-language text was tested. (f) The Presidio equivalence is asserted without running Presidio, and Presidio ships no France-specific recognizers, so neither side of the comparison is known. A GDPR-relevant 'Yes' on this evidence is a real risk if acted on.
